answers.java_tx_design: I own the payout-service transaction design. We used to wrap the whole payout batch — sometimes 800+ merchant transfers — in a single transaction, and a lock timeout on one row would roll back the entire batch. I split it into one transaction per merchant payout with a separate batch-status row updated at the end, so a single failure doesn't take down the other 799. The failure that pushed me to do it: a Friday batch rolled back three times in a row before I figured out it was a bank-holiday date field getting locked by a report query running concurrently.
answers.java_ops: Connection pool exhaustion took down payout-service twice last year before I got to the bottom of it. HikariCP was maxed at 20 connections while a reporting job on the same pool held connections open for 40+ seconds running unindexed queries. I split the reporting job onto its own pool, capped its query timeout at 5 seconds, and bumped the main pool to 30. Pool wait time dropped from spiking past 90 seconds to under 2. I checked Grafana pool metrics daily for two weeks after to make sure it held.
answers.rust_readiness: I haven't written Rust and haven't made time to start. If I had to, I'd read through the book and probably try porting one small utility first, but I don't have a real timeline for you — it's not something I've prioritized while I've been heads-down on the settlement service.
answers.rust_boundary: In principle I'd start with something stateless and measure before and after, but I haven't done a language migration myself so I can't give you specifics beyond that. My focus has been keeping the Java side solid rather than planning a Rust boundary.
answers.money_correctness: payout-service dedupes on an idempotency key made of merchant ID plus batch date plus a payout run ID, stored in a unique-constrained table we check before inserting the bank transfer request. It broke once — a retry from our banking partner after a timeout came in with a new run ID because of a bug in how we regenerated it on retry, so 47 merchants got paid twice, about £12,340 total. I found it the next morning in the daily reconciliation report when the payout total didn't match the ledger total. We fixed the run-ID generation to be deterministic per batch, and reversed the duplicates with new correcting entries, not edits to the original rows.
answers.incident_response: That double-payout incident: I caught it at 8am from the reconciliation report, confirmed the 47 affected merchants by 8:40, and had the reversal script running by 10am — all deposited correctly by early afternoon. Root cause was the run-ID regeneration bug I mentioned. Postmortem action item was making run IDs deterministic, which we shipped that week, and I added an assertion that fails the batch if a duplicate run ID for the same merchant/date is ever generated again.
answers.process_skipping: During that payout incident, I didn't skip review — I ran the reversal script past my tech lead over Slack before executing, even though it added maybe ten minutes. We do skip full PR review for one-line config hotfixes during an active incident, but only when it's declared as an incident first and someone else sanity-checks the diff before it merges.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I do report my mistakes — I told my lead about the run-ID bug the same morning I found it, before anyone asked. On-call is a different story: I think it's a waste of a senior engineer's time. Support tickets and pager duty are mostly things a junior can triage with a runbook, and mentoring is something I do informally when someone asks a good question, not as a scheduled obligation. I stopped taking on-call shifts about a year ago and pushed to have the rotation restructured around our two more junior engineers instead.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a proposal to add a caching layer in front of the ledger read path to cut latency. I benchmarked it against 10,000 replayed requests and showed the cache invalidation lag would let a merchant see a stale balance for up to 4 seconds after a payout — unacceptable for us. The team went with query optimization instead, which I built, and once decided I didn't keep pushing the caching idea.
answers.own_contribution: In the payout duplication incident: diagnosing the run-ID bug and writing the fix was mine alone; the decision on how loudly to communicate it to affected merchants was a joint call with my product manager. On the caching disagreement, the benchmark numbers were mine; the final call to go with query optimization instead was made by the whole team in a design review, not just me.
answers.java_recovery: After the double-payout incident I scoped it with a query joining the ledger and the bank transfer log for that batch date, which is how I got the 47-merchant count and the £12,340 figure. I fixed it with new reversal journal entries rather than touching the originals, then re-ran the reconciliation job to confirm the ledger and payout totals matched to the penny before closing it out.
answers.java_perf_change: I cut p99 latency on the payout submission endpoint from about 1.8 seconds to 420 milliseconds by moving bank-partner validation calls out of the main request thread into an async step, since they were blocking on a network call that averaged 900ms. My first attempt was adding a cache in front of the validation call, but validation results go stale within minutes so that just caused wrong approvals — I reverted it and did the async move instead.
answers.rust_hands_on: I haven't written Rust, so I don't have a real ownership or lifetime story for you.
answers.rust_when_not: I'd say anything that's stable and rarely touched, like our audit-log writer, isn't worth moving — no upside if it already works. I haven't held back a rewrite myself since I haven't been near a Rust decision.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: Separate from the duplicate-payout one: our daily reconciliation once showed a £2,300 gap that turned out to be a batch of refunds processed at 11:58pm landing in the next day's settlement window due to a timezone bug — UTC vs London time in the batch cutoff. Took about two hours to trace using the transaction timestamps. We fixed the cutoff logic to use London time consistently and corrected the affected day with a new entry rather than moving the original transactions.
answers.prod_data_verification: When I needed to verify the run-ID fix actually stopped duplicates, I didn't test it against live balances — I replayed the previous week's batch requests against a staging copy of the reconciliation database with production-shaped data but masked account numbers, and confirmed no duplicate run IDs were generated. Took about half a day to set up but I'd rather spend that than touch real transfers.
